title: Manuscript citation audit
text:
NoteScope and method (17 November 2026)



Every citation-bearing sentence and table cell in journal.typ (Introduction through Conclusion, including Table 1) and in supplement Tables S2 and S3 was checked against the archived sources, following llm-wiki/AGENTS.md: catalog → evidence record → raw passage, and the archived PDF wherever numbers, tables, figures or garbled extraction mattered. Bibliography integrity (missing/unused keys, metadata vs. PDF) was checked for both files. Earlier audits were re-checked against the current text: journal Table 1 (claim-audits/table-1.md), Table S2 (claim-audits/table-2.md) and Table S3.
The three high-severity manuscript findings and the two high-severity Sanyal findings below were re-verified directly against the PDFs (Mikheev Fig. 6, Petek Table 3, Sanyal Table 1). Verdicts are conservative; where the archive is silent, the item is marked Not verifiable rather than filled in.

A. Introduction and Related Work

Summary
Claims checked: 45 (all cited sources are archived).

Most important issues:

A2 (High), journal.typ:70–73. The numbers “52% created topoplots, second only to ERP waveforms (61%)” do not appear anywhere in Mikheev et al. (2024). In Figure 6, 175 of 213 respondents (82%) had plotted a topoplot and 187 of 213 (88%) had plotted an ERP plot. The ranking (second) is correct; both percentages are wrong.
A17 (High), Table 1, Petek row. The cell says “for only 5 of the 18 visualizations did at least one tool provide built-in support for quantifying uncertainty”. In Petek Table 3, only 3 of 18 rows have a quantifying wrapper (✓). The 5 rows are those with ✓ or ◦, and ◦ means the user must still quantify uncertainty. The 13/18 (72%) all-× count is correct. This error was introduced after the 26 Oct audit.
A4 (High), journal.typ:86–89. The Introduction says Allen’s 20% applies to “data with more than three features”. Allen’s “3D” graphics have exactly three variables (two independent and one dependent; Fig. 1A). The 20% is correct, but the population it describes is misstated.
A36 (Moderate), journal.typ:266–268. Perceptual studies that “identify areas with high uncertainty … accuracy and response time” are attributed to Hullman et al. (2015). That HOPs study asked people to estimate properties of 1–3 distributions, with no spatial search. The description fits Sanyal et al. (2009), which is already in refs.bib.
A41 (Moderate), journal.typ:291–292. “In ERP waveforms, uncertainty is commonly shown using error bars or shaded confidence intervals”. The three cited sources give examples (Kappenman: ±1 SEM shading, not a CI; Pernet: bootstrap 95% CI; Allen: a recommended CI band, with the typical ERP panel described as having “no portrayal of uncertainty”). None of them shows how common this practice is. Mikheev’s 40% without error bars points the other way.
A8 (Low), Table 1, Allen row. The 26 Oct audit’s single recommended wording correction (“Only 20% of audited 3D graphics portrayed uncertainty”) has still not been applied.

correll2018task

journal.typ:273–274
fernandes2018uncertainty
“measured decision quality through expected payoffs”
Supported

raw/fernandes2018uncertainty.md#p007-b002 (“Decision Metric: expected/optimal payoff”)
—

greis2015investigating

journal.typ:291–292

“In ERP waveforms, uncertainty is commonly shown using error bars or shaded confidence intervals”
Overstated

journal.typ:292–294
pernet2011limo
scalp maps can display “test statistics or significance markers, but these do not directly show uncertainty in the estimated voltage”
Supported
—
raw/pernet2011limo.md#p008-b006 (Fig. 4 B2 “topographic plot of F values”)
— (the “do not directly show” clause is the manuscript’s inference)

journal.typ:296–299
pernet2011limo

Supported

raw/pernet2011limo.md#p005-b002 (“construct robust confidence intervals for each electrode and each frame”); #p008-b006 (Fig. 4: A1/A2 CI waveforms, B2 F-value topography)
—

journal.typ:299–301
gerslova2026diegr

Supported

raw/gerslova2026diegr.md#p041-b003, #p042-b004 (“three panels: CI lower, mean, CI upper”)

journal.typ:303–305
pernet2011limo; gerslova2026diegr
“Neither publication systematically evaluates how users interpret different visualization designs”
Supported

Absence claim, checked against the archived texts: pernet2011limo is a methods/toolbox paper (#p001-b008); gerslova2026diegr is a CRAN reference manual (#p001-b001). Neither contains a user study.

By severity, for findings that are not Supported: High 3, Moderate 11, Low 11.
Most important issues:

Sanyal et al., Table S3 (High). Two lower-order rankings contradict or go beyond the paper’s Table 1 (PDF p. 7). The paper reports only significant pairwise contrasts. It gives no per-task means: Figs. 10–11 pool across tasks.

1D least-uncertain: S3 says “glyph colour ≈ surface colour > error bars”, but the paper reports that error bars beat surface colour.
1D most-uncertain: S3 says “glyph size > error bars”, but no such difference is reported.

Correll et al. 2018, E2 (High). S3 ranks VSUPs as “best-performing” in the Battleship task. The paper found no effect on mean uncertainty of placements. VSUPs avoided the most uncertain cells (KS test), but their placements carried higher average danger, i.e. lower expected value. The earlier S3 audit’s qualification (“not a universal decision advantage”) is not reflected.
Kale et al. E2 N = 150 (Moderate; Not verifiable). The archived paper does not state the E2 sample. The figure comes only from the authors’ external CSV, which is not archived, and the cell carries no source note.
Greis et al. Data = M (Moderate; Not supported by the archive). The archived paper never states whether the rainfall/forecast data were real or simulated. The M code rests on the dissertation, which is not archived.
Wainer & Francolini N (Moderate). S2 gives only “N: 16”. Experiment 2, which S3 ranks separately, used 8 returning participants. The S2 caption says separate values are shown when samples differ.
Several S3 cells overstate a winner or tie.

Correll & Gleicher E1 (Moderate): box plots tied bar charts on confidence.
Gschwandtner “E3b” (Moderate): centred error bars alone were significantly best.
Sterzik E2 (Moderate): the authors call texture, waves, contours, colour and hulls “similar”, not ordered.
Sterzik E3 (Moderate): texture ties colour on SES, and colour wins on sticks.
Kusumastuti (Moderate): the table omits that E2 practice used the ellipse display.
Scholz (Moderate): “mean rank 3.35” is actually a preference score, where 4 means most preferred.

section: F9. Completion times were joined to the wrong trials

F9. Completion times were joined to the wrong trials

Severity: Critical · Area: Task 1 and Task 2 completion time

Problem. SoSci Survey records “Time spent on page xxx”, and each trial page keeps its questionnaire number when the display order is randomized. The pages treated TIME005:TIME025 and TIME029:TIME049 as times at presentation positions, so every time was attached to the wrong trial. All time tables, violin plots, time models, and the Task 1 time–accuracy model were wrong.
Resolution.

Times are now joined on trial = page − 4 (Task 1) and trial = page − 28 (Task 2). The presentation position comes from the logged display order.
Both analyses moved to the new Time analysis page. The Task 1 and Task 2 trial reconstructions are shared scripts (scripts/task1_trials.R, scripts/task2_trials.R).
Each task has a visible check plot of time by presentation position. It shows the expected learning curve: the first trial shown is the slowest (Task 2: about 31 s, falling to about 11 s).
The Task 1 time–accuracy sentences are now generated from the confidence intervals.

Corrected results (geometric-mean time for a typical participant):




Fastest
Slowest




Task 1
Basic 10.6 s
Bivariate corner 15.3 s, Adjacent 14.6 s


Task 2
Basic 10.3 s
Bivariate corner 16.7 s



Task 1 time–accuracy, corrected:

Within participants, slower trials were less often answered correctly.
After adjustment, generally slower participants were more accurate.

title: Fixed
section: F1. A304 aesthetic-rating labels were wrong
text:
F1. A304 aesthetic-rating labels were wrong

Severity: Critical · Area: Subjective ratings

Problem. In the export, A304 is stored in the display order but with nonsequential suffixes (A304_01, _06, _02, _03, _04, _05, _07). Reading the suffix as the display position mislabeled five of the seven aesthetic conditions.
Resolution.

title: Fixed
section: F2. Task 1 ignored repeated comparison items
text:
F2. Task 1 ignored repeated comparison items

Severity: High · Area: Task 1 accuracy model

Problem. The accuracy model treated responses as independent given the participant, although target and distractor images recur across participants.
Resolution.

The primary model is correct ~ vistype + pattern + position_c + (1 | ID) + (1 | stimulus) + (1 | wrong_image).
Reported probabilities are averaged over the three ERP patterns and integrated over the participant, target, and distractor distributions.
The Gauss–Hermite integration matches numerical integration to within 2 × 10⁻⁷.
A participant-specific position slope was singular and is documented.

title: Fixed
section: F3. Analytic sample definition
text:
F3. Analytic sample definition

Severity: High · Area: Data preparation

Problem. Inclusion does not require the survey’s formal completion marker.
Resolution.

The analytic sample is defined as all respondents who completed every primary endpoint: 146 at present.
All have 21 Task 1 responses, 21 Task 2 responses, and 28 ratings.
59 are marked unfinished but stopped after the last outcome page.
Describe them as endpoint-complete respondents rather than as formal completions.

title: Unresolved
section: U7. Task 2 scores are not comparable across stimuli
text:
U7. Task 2 scores are not comparable across stimuli

Severity: Moderate · Area: Task 2 outcome

Problem. Region values are min–max rescaled within each stimulus, so the same score means different things for different stimuli. For example, the 10th-best region scores between 0.24 and 0.90 depending on the stimulus.
Evidence.

Rank outcome: Bivariate corner −0.21, p = .002.
Top-3 logistic outcome: no visualization effect reaches p < .05.

Fix. Report a rank or top-k sensitivity analysis, and avoid interpreting score magnitudes across stimuli.
Open question. For 4 of 10 P3 stimuli, the most chosen region (R25) ranks only 10th–14th by score. Participants may target the voltage peak rather than the SNR peak. That is a construct-validity question for the scoring.

title: Unresolved
section: U8. Multiplicity is handled inconsistently
text:
U8. Multiplicity is handled inconsistently

Severity: Moderate · Area: All inferential results

Problem. No primary contrasts or multiplicity families are defined, and the same contrast is shown under different adjustments.

Task 2, Bivariate corner vs Basic:

Tukey table: p = .070.
Dunnett figure: interval [−7.2, −0.3] pp, which excludes zero.
Coefficient table: unadjusted p = .005.

Task 1: unadjusted coefficient p-values are reported.
Ratings: the contrast figure is Dunnett-adjusted but labelled only “95% confidence intervals”. Four outcomes × six contrasts have no stated family.

Fix. Choose the primary contrasts and one adjustment family (for example, Dunnett against Basic within each outcome). Use it in every table and figure and name it in captions. Report all estimates, including null results.

title: Unresolved
section: U9. Rating models: intercept only, proportional odds violated
text:
U9. Rating models: intercept only, proportional odds violated

Severity: Moderate · Area: Subjective-rating models

Problem.

The cumulative-link models use rating_ord ~ vistype + (1 | ID), although each participant rates every visualization.
Likelihood-ratio tests on fixed-effects clm fits reject proportional odds for all four questions (p = .011 to 3 × 10⁻⁵).
Model-based expected ratings differ from raw means by at most 0.08.

Fix.

Evaluate participant-specific visualization effects, or justify the simpler structure with a sensitivity analysis.
Report the proportional-odds check, and describe the estimates as model-smoothed means.

title: Unresolved
section: U10. Composite ranking and “leader” highlighting
text:
U10. Composite ranking and “leader” highlighting

Severity: Moderate · Area: Subjective ratings

Problem.

Composite. “Sum of mean ratings” adds four separately measured criteria with equal weight. One of them is a likelihood-of-use item (U3), and one was asked at a different time (U4).

With participant-bootstrap intervals, neighbouring ranks overlap. For example, Uncertainty markers 12.28 [11.62, 12.88] vs Basic 12.24 [11.70, 12.82].

Leader highlighting. is_leader highlights Confidence intervals for “comparison”. Its difference from Basic is +0.18 [−0.09, 0.45], and its differences from the runners-up were never tested.

Fix. Remove the composite, or show it with intervals and label it as an exploratory equal-weight index. Highlight a leader only if pairwise contrasts support it.

title: Unresolved
section: U11. Time outliers and the time estimand
text:
U11. Time outliers and the time estimand

Severity: Moderate · Area: Task 1 and Task 2 completion time

Problem.

Different data. The descriptive tables on the Time analysis page drop trials with a per-visualization 1.5 × IQR rule. The models keep everything, including pages of 5,264 s and 11,221 s.
Mislabelled estimate. The back-transformed model estimate is a geometric mean (median time for a typical participant), but it is labelled “estimated time”.

Fix.

Define one outlier rule in advance and apply it to tables and models.
Show the alternative as a sensitivity analysis.
Label the estimate as a geometric mean.

title: Unresolved
section: U12. Qualitative coding is not validated
text:
U12. Qualitative coding is not validated

Severity: Moderate · Area: Open-ended feedback

Problem. The A305 coding comes from a single LLM coder, with no second coder or agreement statistic.

Rule not applied. Generic “bivariate plots” comments are sometimes coded to both Corner and Range instead of General bivariates (IDs 7, 41, 77).
Duplicated units. 51 of 298 rows (17%) are one unit duplicated across visualizations.
Scale use. Only 2 of 298 units are coded 0.
Sparse cells. 31 of 69 theme × visualization rows rest on two or fewer participants, yet are shown with means to two decimals.

Fix.

Have a human double-code at least a subsample and report agreement.
Enforce the General-bivariates rule.
Flag or suppress cells with n ≤ 2.

text:
U13. Fixed item order in the rating questions

Severity: Moderate (design limitation) · Area: Subjective ratings

Problem. Within every rating question the visualizations appear in the same order: Adjacent first, Basic always last. Order and context effects cannot be separated from visualization effects.
Fix. Report this as a limitation in the manuscript.

text:
U14. Sample definition and data quality are undocumented

Severity: Low · Area: Data preparation

Problem.

Excluded by the date cutoff: four completed records dated 2026-07-23, probably pilot runs, are excluded without documentation.
Possible quality problems:

five participants exceed SoSci’s speeding index (TIME_RSI > 2);

title: Table S3 literature audit
text:
This audit supports the criterion-specific rankings added to Supplementary Table S3. It covers the 13 empirical evaluations already listed in Supplementary Table S2. A ranking is reported only when the paper provides a point-estimate order, an inferential comparison, or an explicit author conclusion. ≈ denotes a tie, an inconclusive contrast, or no reliable difference; it does not assert numerical equality. Partial orders are retained where the paper does not support a complete ranking.
The archived PDFs were inspected for every table- or figure-based ranking. This was especially important for Sanyal et al., whose extracted text has a broken font mapping.

Table S3 row

Wainer & Francolini (1980)
Experiment 1 results; legend-removal results
Accuracy and response time favor different displays.


Sanyal et al. (2009)
Closing discussion; archived PDF, pp. 7–9, especially Table 1 and Figs. 10–11
Rankings are descriptive means and differ between 1D and 2D tasks; no universal winner.


MacEachren et al. (2012)
Experiment 1 design/results; Experiment 2 Table 4; response-time interpretation
Iconicity had no consistent accuracy effect; abstract symbols were faster overall but not in every category.


Correll & Gleicher (2014)
one-sample likelihood results; confidence results; discussion
The evidence supports a contrast between bar charts and the symmetric alternatives, not a reliable ordering among the alternatives.


Scholz & Lu (2014)
preference ranks; decision case
Only the preference task ranks the four encodings; the decision case is not a between-encoding comparison.


Greis et al. (2015)
survey means; game outcomes and preferences
Survey ratings and behavioral performance are reported separately; the game sample was only 12.


Hullman et al. (2015)
completion time; task-specific errors
HOPs dominate multi-variable ordering tasks but not every one-variable estimate; the time difference was not significant.


Gschwandtner et al. (2016)
error tests, Tables 1–2; task-specific results, Fig. 6; interpretation results
Boundary, duration, probability, and time tasks yield different orders.


Correll et al. (2018)
identification conditions and Fig. 6; identification and decision results
E1 supports discrete superposition; E2 supports a change in uncertainty-sensitive choices, not a universal decision advantage.


Fernandes et al. (2018)
learning and consistency results; final-trial comparison
Dot50 is the clearest winner; the paper does not establish a complete order among all lower-performing conditions.


Kale et al. (2019)
E1 JND result; E2 JND result; E2 qualifications
Regular HOPs beat the static comparator in each experiment; the fast-HOP contrast with line ensembles was inconclusive.


Kusumastuti et al. (2023)
E1 post-practice results; E2 post-practice results
Practice and number of sources alter the ordering; the E2 ellipse advantage follows practice with ellipse stimuli.


Sterzik et al. (2025)
directionality results; value-estimation results; cross-study interpretation; conclusion
Directionality and value-estimation criteria favor different metaphors; the lower-order ranking changes by molecular representation.
